name: Core Filesystem
description: Protects against recursive rm commands and equivalent filesystem destruction outside literal temp subdirectories

destructive_patterns.name: sed-exec-unverified
destructive_patterns.description: GNU sed executes shell input that the engine cannot statically verify.
destructive_patterns.explanation: Use a literal sed replacement or inspect the fully rendered shell command before allowing execution. Backreferences, '&', and an empty `e` command depend on runtime input.

destructive_patterns.name: cp-sensitive-then-delete
destructive_patterns.description: archive copy of a sensitive path into temp followed by forced recursive deletion is a cross-segment data-loss bypass. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`cp -al /etc /tmp/x && rm -rf /tmp/x` is a propagation variant of the \ relocate-then-delete bypass: the copy segment is allowed, and the temp \ delete segment is normally safe, but the compound command can destroy \ sensitive content or hide irreversible deletion behind a temp path.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Copy beside the original or into a named backup path and verify with `diff -r`. \ - Do not combine sensitive-source propagation and forced deletion in one command. \ - Use `rm -ri` if a derived temp tree genuinely needs manual cleanup.

destructive_patterns.name: ln-symlink-sensitive-then-delete
destructive_patterns.description: symlink from a sensitive path into temp followed by forced recursive deletion can traverse and destroy the target. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`ln -s /etc /tmp/x && rm -rf /tmp/x/.` can turn an apparently safe temp \ cleanup into deletion through a symlink. The temp path does not make the \ operation safe once it points back at a sensitive tree.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Inspect symlinks with `readlink` and `ls -la` before removing anything. \ - Remove only the link itself with `unlink /tmp/<link>` when that is the intent. \ - Avoid combining symlink creation and recursive deletion in one command.

destructive_patterns.name: rsync-sensitive-then-delete
destructive_patterns.description: rsync archive of a sensitive path into temp followed by forced recursive deletion is a cross-segment data-loss bypass. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`rsync -a /etc/ /tmp/dest/ && rm -rf /tmp/dest` is the rsync form of the \ sensitive-source propagation bypass. Archive mode preserves enough structure \ that the later temp cleanup should require human review.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Run rsync and inspect the destination in a separate step. \ - Use `--dry-run` for rsync previews. \ - Use `rm -ri` for manual cleanup of derived temp trees.

destructive_patterns.name: rm-rf-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: rm -rf on root or home paths is EXTREMELY DANGEROUS. This command will NOT be executed. Ask the user to run it manually if truly needed.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
This command would recursively delete files starting from the root filesystem (/) \ or home directory (~). This is catastrophic and will destroy:

\ - Your entire operating system \ - All installed applications and libraries \ - All user data, documents, and configurations \ - Boot files, making the system unbootable

\ There is NO recovery without backups. Even with backups, full restoration \ takes hours to days.

\ If you need to delete specific files, use explicit paths: \ rm -rf /path/to/specific/directory

\ Always preview what would be deleted first: \ find /path/to/directory -type f | head -20

destructive_patterns.name: rm-r-f-separate-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: rm with separate -r -f flags targeting root or home is EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Separate `-r -f` flags on `/` or `~` have identical effect to `rm -rf /`: \ recursive, forced, silent deletion of the entire filesystem or home directory.

\ There is NO recovery without backups. Run only if truly intended.

destructive_patterns.name: rm-recursive-force-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: rm --recursive --force targeting root or home is EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation: The long-flag form has identical effect to `rm -rf /`: recursive, forced, \ silent deletion. Run only if truly intended.

destructive_patterns.name: rm-rf-general
destructive_patterns.description: rm -rf is destructive and requires human approval. Explain what you want to delete and why, then ask the user to run the command manually.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
rm -rf recursively removes files and directories without confirmation prompts. \ The -f (force) flag suppresses all warnings, making accidental deletions \ silent and immediate.

\ Why this is dangerous: \ - Deleted files bypass the trash - they're gone immediately \ - Typos in paths can delete unintended directories \ - Wildcards can expand to match more than expected \ - No undo mechanism exists

\ Safe alternatives: \ - rm -ri: Interactive mode, confirms each file \ - trash-cli: Moves files to trash instead of deleting \ - rm -rf in literal /tmp or /var/tmp subdirectories: Allowed \ - Variable-rooted paths such as $TMPDIR: Reviewed because the environment may point anywhere

\ Preview what would be deleted: \ find /path/to/delete -type f | wc -l # Count files \ ls -la /path/to/delete # List contents

destructive_patterns.name: rm-glob-home
destructive_patterns.description: rm with an unexpanded glob under a home directory deletes an unbounded, shell-chosen file set and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
The glob is expanded by the shell at execution time, so the author cannot \ review the exact file set being deleted: `rm -f ~/Downloads/*.md` removes \ every matching file, exactly like the already-blocked recursive forms.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Preview the expansion first: `ls ~/Downloads/*.md` \ - Delete explicitly named files: `rm ~/Downloads/one-file.md` \ - Move to trash instead: `mv ~/Downloads/*.md ~/.local/share/Trash/`

destructive_patterns.name: rm-r-f-separate
destructive_patterns.description: rm with separate -r -f flags is destructive and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
rm with separate -r and -f flags has the same effect as rm -rf: recursive \ forced deletion without confirmation.

\ Common variations that are all equivalent: \ - rm -r -f path \ - rm -f -r path \ - rm -r -f -v path (verbose but still forced)

\ All carry the same risks as rm -rf: immediate, silent, irreversible deletion.

\ This rule matches the -r/-f flag PAIR, not a filesystem path, so it also \ fires when `rm` is another tool's subcommand (`git rm -r -f`, \ `bq rm -r -f`). The recursive-force semantics still apply, but to that \ tool's objects — tracked files and index entries for git, a dataset and \ everything in it for bq — not to a directory tree. Enable that tool's pack \ for guidance written for it; this rule is the backstop when it is not.

\ Safer approach for temporary directories: \ - rm -r -f /tmp/mydir # Allowed - temp directories are safe \ - Resolve and inspect $TMPDIR before using it as a deletion root

\ For other paths, prefer: \ rm -ri /path # Interactive confirmation

destructive_patterns.name: rm-recursive-force-long
destructive_patterns.description: rm --recursive --force is destructive and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
rm --recursive --force is the long-form equivalent of rm -rf. While more \ readable, it carries identical risks: silent, recursive, irreversible deletion.

\ The long flags may appear in: \ - Scripts aiming for clarity \ - Generated code from build tools \ - Cross-platform compatibility scenarios

\ All standard rm -rf precautions apply: \ - Verify the path before running \ - Use absolute paths to avoid ambiguity \ - Consider using trash-cli for recoverable deletion

\ Preview command: \ find /path --maxdepth 2 -ls | head -30

destructive_patterns.name: find-delete-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: find <sensitive-path> -delete is bytewise-equivalent to rm -rf on root/home and is EXTREMELY DANGEROUS. This command will NOT be executed.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`find <path> -delete` is the bytewise-equivalent of `rm -rf <path>`: \ it recursively removes every file and (when -depth is implied) every \ directory matched by the predicate. Targeting `/`, `~`, `$HOME`, or any \ top-level system directory (`/etc`, `/usr`, `/var`, `/home`, `/boot`, \ `/dev`, `/proc`, `/sys`, `/lib`, `/lib64`, `/opt`, `/root`) destroys \ the operating system or user data the same way `rm -rf` would.

\ There is NO recovery without backups.

\ If you only need to delete files matching a pattern, use a much more \ specific path: \ find /path/to/specific/subdir -name '*.tmp' -delete

\ Always preview first: \ find /path -type f | head -20

destructive_patterns.name: find-delete-general
destructive_patterns.description: find ... -delete is destructive (bytewise-equivalent to rm -rf on the matched tree) and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`find ... -delete` recursively deletes every path matched by the find \ expression. The action flag `-delete` implies `-depth` (so directories \ are deleted after their contents). With no path predicate it deletes \ the entire starting tree. Common pitfalls:

\ - `find . -delete` deletes the current working directory's contents. \ - `find <path> -delete` with a wide -name glob matches more than expected. \ - `-delete` errors are silent by default — failures don't stop the walk.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Drop -delete to preview: `find <path> ...` (just lists matches) \ - Add -print -delete to log each deletion as it happens \ - Use `find /tmp/<subdir> ... -delete` (allowed under temp dirs) \ - For a few files: `find ... | xargs -t -p rm -i` for confirmation

destructive_patterns.name: unlink-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: unlink on a sensitive system or home path is one-shot data destruction with no recovery. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`unlink <file>` is the raw POSIX unlink(2) primitive: it removes a single \ directory entry without prompting, without trash, without backup. On a \ sensitive system file (`/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers`) or \ a home-directory key (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `$HOME/.gnupg/...`) the result \ is irrecoverable.

\ There is NO recovery without backups.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - `mv <file> <file>.deleted-YYYYMMDD` then verify nothing breaks, then \ `unlink <file>.deleted-...` after a few days. \ - `cp <file> <file>.bak && unlink <file>` to keep an explicit backup. \ - `unlink /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed (temp dirs).

destructive_patterns.name: unlink-general
destructive_patterns.description: unlink is destructive (POSIX equivalent of rm on a single file) and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`unlink <file>` removes a single directory entry without confirmation, \ without trash, without backup. While not as broad as `rm -rf`, a typo in \ the target path destroys an unintended file.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Verify the path with `ls -la <file>` first. \ - Make a backup: `cp <file> <file>.bak`. \ - For temp scratch: `unlink /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed. \ - Use `mv <file> /tmp/quarantine-<file>` if you want a delayed delete.

destructive_patterns.name: truncate-zero-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: truncate with a potentially shrinking size on a sensitive system or home path destroys data. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`truncate -s 0 <file>` zeros a file in place. `truncate -s -<N> <file>` \ shrinks a file by N bytes (destroying the trailing data). On a sensitive \ system file (`/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers`) or a home-\ directory key/credential the result is irrecoverable.

\ There is NO recovery without backups.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Make a backup first: `cp <file> <file>.bak && truncate -s 0 <file>`. \ - For growth (NOT shrink): `truncate -s +<N>` is allowed (no data loss). \ - For temp scratch: `truncate -s 0 /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed.

destructive_patterns.name: truncate-zero-general
destructive_patterns.description: truncate with an absolute or shrinking size can destroy file content and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`truncate -s 0 <file>` zeros a file in place; `truncate -s -<N> <file>` \ shrinks it by N bytes. Both destroy data without confirmation, without \ trash, without backup. While not as broad as `rm`, a typo in the target \ path destroys an unintended file.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Verify the size first: `wc -c <file>`. \ - Make a backup: `cp <file> <file>.bak && truncate -s 0 <file>`. \ - For growth: `truncate -s +<N>` (allowed; non-destructive). \ - For temp scratch: `truncate -s 0 /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed.

destructive_patterns.name: shred-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: shred on a sensitive system or home path destroys data beyond forensic recovery. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`shred` overwrites file content with random data (DoD-style multi-pass by \ default). With `-u`/`--remove`/`-fzu` the file is also unlinked. On a \ sensitive system file (`/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers`) or a \ home-directory key/credential the result is unrecoverable even with \ specialised forensics — that is shred's entire design intent.

\ There is NO recovery without backups.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Verify the path with `ls -la <file>` first. \ - Make a backup: `cp <file> <file>.bak && shred -u <file>`. \ - For temp scratch: `shred -u /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed. \ - For modern SSDs, single-pass is sufficient: `shred -n 1 -u <file>`.

destructive_patterns.name: shred-general
destructive_patterns.description: shred destroys file content beyond recovery and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`shred` overwrites file content with random data; `-u`/`--remove` adds an \ unlink step. The whole point is that the data cannot be recovered. While \ not as broad as `rm -rf`, a typo in the target path destroys an unintended \ file with no possibility of undo.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Verify the path with `ls -la <file>` first. \ - Make a backup: `cp <file> <file>.bak`. \ - For temp scratch: `shred -u /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed. \ - On modern SSDs `shred` may not actually overwrite the underlying flash \ cells; use `cryptsetup erase` or vendor secure-erase utilities instead.

destructive_patterns.name: tar-remove-files-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: tar --remove-files on a sensitive system or home path is recursive deletion masquerading as an archive operation. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`tar --remove-files -cf <archive> <source>` first archives the source paths \ into <archive>, then deletes the originals. With a sensitive source \ (`/etc`, `/usr`, `/var`, `/home/<user>`, `~`, `$HOME`, ...) the result is \ bytewise-equivalent to `rm -rf <source>`. With `-cf /dev/null` the archive \ is discarded entirely, making this a pure recursive delete with no audit \ trail.

\ There is NO recovery without backups.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Drop `--remove-files`: `tar -cf out.tar <source>` (sources preserved). \ - Two-step with confirmation: `tar -cf out.tar <source> && rm -ri <source>`. \ - Verify the source first: `ls -la <source>`. \ - Allowed for temp dirs: `tar --remove-files -cf out.tar /tmp/<subdir>`.

destructive_patterns.name: tar-remove-files-general
destructive_patterns.description: tar --remove-files deletes source paths after archiving and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`tar --remove-files <source>` deletes the source paths once they have been \ archived. While not as broad as `rm -rf`, a typo or wide glob in the source \ list destroys files the agent did not intend to remove. With `-cf /dev/null` \ the archive itself is discarded — the operation becomes a pure delete.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Drop `--remove-files` to preserve sources after archiving. \ - Verify the source list with `ls -la` before running. \ - For temp scratch: `tar --remove-files -cf out.tar /tmp/<subdir>` is allowed.

destructive_patterns.name: dd-overwrite-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: dd of=<sensitive-path> overwrites file contents in place. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS on a system or home file.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`dd if=/dev/zero of=<file>` and `dd if=/dev/urandom of=<file>` overwrite the \ file's contents in place — the `truncate -s 0` equivalent at the dd layer. \ On a sensitive system file (`/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers`) or \ a home-directory key/credential the result is irrecoverable. Even without an \ explicit input source (`dd of=<file>` reads from stdin), the file's content \ is destroyed.

\ There is NO recovery without backups.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Make a backup first: `cp <file> <file>.bak && dd if=/dev/zero of=<file>`. \ - For read-only verification: `dd if=<file> of=/dev/null` (output discarded). \ - For temp scratch: `dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed.

\ Device-level dd (`dd of=/dev/sda`) is governed by the `system.disk` pack \ — enable it for partition-table protection.

destructive_patterns.name: dd-overwrite-general
destructive_patterns.description: dd with of=<file> overwrites file contents and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`dd of=<file>` overwrites the file's contents (with the input from `if=` \ or stdin if no input source is given). While not as broad as `rm -rf`, a \ typo in the target path destroys an unintended file with no possibility of \ undo.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Verify the path first: `ls -la <file>`. \ - Make a backup: `cp <file> <file>.bak && dd if=/dev/zero of=<file>`. \ - Read-only verification: `dd if=<file> of=/dev/null`. \ - For temp scratch: `dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed. \ - For device writes: enable the `system.disk` pack.

destructive_patterns.name: mv-sensitive-source-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: mv touching a sensitive system or home path is the cross-segment recursive-force-delete bypass. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`mv /etc /tmp/x && rm -rf /tmp/x` is the canonical cross-segment bypass: \ each segment is individually allowed (mv-to-tmp is benign; rm-rf-in-tmp \ is safe) but the pair destroys `/etc`. The same shape closes via \ `mv /etc /dev/null`, `mv $HOME /tmp/x`, or any "relocate then delete" chain.

\ Any mv that mentions a sensitive path (source OR destination — `/etc`, \ `/usr`, `/var`, `/home`, `~`, `$HOME`, ...) blocks here, including \ in-place renames within /etc.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Backup with copy + verify + delete: \ `cp -a <source> <source>.bak && diff -r <source> <source>.bak && rm -rf <source>` \ - Soft-delete via in-place rename: `mv <file> <file>.deleted-YYYYMMDD` \ (use `the engine allow-once` for the rename, then a follow-up `rm` after a soak period). \ - Pure tmp-to-tmp moves: `mv /tmp/<a> /tmp/<b>` is allowed.

destructive_patterns.name: mv-dynamic-path
destructive_patterns.description: mv with a shell-expanded or escaped path cannot be verified before execution.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Shell variables and command substitutions are controlled by the calling environment and may resolve to `/`, `/etc`, a home directory, or another persistent tree. Backslash escapes can also hide traversal from lexical path checks, so the engine cannot safely classify this move.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Resolve and inspect every path before moving it. \ - Use an explicit literal `/tmp/<subdir>` or `/var/tmp/<subdir>` path. \ - Use `the engine allow-once` only after verifying the resolved source and destination.

destructive_patterns.name: redirect-truncate-root-home
destructive_patterns.description: shell truncating redirect (including arbitrary numeric, named, and PowerShell all-stream forms) to a sensitive system or home path destroys the previous file contents. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`> /etc/passwd` (or `: > /etc/passwd`, `echo > /etc/passwd`, etc.) opens \ the target file with O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC — the contents are destroyed \ before any write happens. This applies equally to `>|` (force-overwrite), \ `&>` / `>&` (stdout+stderr to file), and numbered FD forms (`1>`, `2>`, `1>|`, \ `2>|`). All of these are silent, immediate, irrecoverable.

\ There is NO recovery without backups.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use append (`>>`) to preserve existing content: `echo line >> <file>`. \ - Make a backup: `cp <file> <file>.bak && echo data > <file>`. \ - For temp scratch: `> /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed. \ - Read redirects (`< <file>`) are not affected — they don't truncate.

destructive_patterns.name: redirect-truncate-dynamic-path
destructive_patterns.description: shell redirect to a dynamic or escaped path may truncate a sensitive file and requires human approval.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
The redirect target is expanded by the shell at runtime, so the engine cannot prove where it points before the file is opened with O_TRUNC.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Resolve and inspect the target path first. \ - Use a literal `/tmp/<subdir>/scratch` path for disposable output. \ - Use append (`>>`) when preserving existing content is acceptable.

destructive_patterns.name: fork-bomb
destructive_patterns.description: This is a fork bomb: it recursively spawns processes until the system is unusable.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
A fork bomb defines a function that pipes itself into itself in the \ background and then calls it. Process count grows exponentially until \ the kernel can no longer schedule anything; the machine typically \ needs a hard reboot, losing all unsaved work in every application.

\ There is no legitimate reason to run this shape. If you are testing \ process limits, use `ulimit -u` in a disposable VM or container.
